Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Violence: Violence, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds, Loss of Control: Lack of control
  Maladaptive Strategies: Revenge Fantasies: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening, Hopelessness: I have no future

Vignette:
Kwame is a 21-year-old Ghanaian-American man who works as a line chef at a mid-range restaurant in a mid-sized American city. He came to the intake appointment alone, dressed neatly, and spoke in measured sentences that occasionally stopped mid-thought, as though the words had somewhere else to be.

Several months ago, Kwame was sexually assaulted by two men he had encountered after a late shift. The assault took place in a narrow alleyway behind the restaurant where he worked, and it was prolonged. Throughout it, one of the men kept a hand pressed to Kwame's chest, pinning him against a wall, while the other moved around him. There was the sound of a car idling at the alley's entrance — engine noise that did not stop — and at several points Kwame heard shouting from the street that came to nothing. He was unable to move, unable to call out effectively, unable to change what was happening. When it was over, he walked back through the restaurant's rear entrance, clocked out, and did not tell anyone.

In the weeks that followed, Kwame continued working the dinner service, because stopping felt like conceding something he could not name. But the kitchen had changed for him. The clatter of pans, a colleague moving quickly behind him, the sound of delivery trucks idling in the alley outside — any of these could collapse the distance between then and now without warning. He would be plating a dish and then, without transition, he would hear the engine again, low and continuous inside his head, and the full weight of that night would be present in his body before his mind had caught up. When this happened he could not always explain to his sous-chef why his hands had gone still. If someone asked him directly about the incident — a counsellor at a free clinic he visited once — he would begin to speak and then lose the thread entirely, the account fragmenting before he could finish a sentence, leaving him staring at the floor.

What Kwame had come to believe about himself in the aftermath was perhaps the most corrosive part of his current experience. He was certain that another man — a stronger man, a more decisive man — would have found a way to stop what happened. He had acted, he felt, in ways that went against everything he understood himself to be, and the shame of that conviction had settled into him like a permanent low temperature. He spent time, particularly at night, constructing elaborate mental scenarios in which he confronted the men responsible, scenarios that were violent and detailed and that provided a few minutes of something that felt like agency before dissolving. He had come to believe, with a quiet and terrible certainty, that there was no future available to him — not in any meaningful sense — and this belief sat beneath everything else like a false floor.

His body had become a site of constant surveillance. He checked himself regularly for signs of injury or wrongness, scanning in a way he could not always explain. At home, in the apartment he shared with a cousin, he could not settle. He remained alert even in rooms he had lived in for two years, tracking the movement of shadows, registering his cousin's sudden gestures as potential threats before correcting himself. He had begun arriving late to shifts and leaving early, not because he had decided to but because the accumulation of small moments — a car sound from the alley, a colleague stepping into his peripheral vision too quickly — had made the full shift increasingly difficult to complete. His supervisor had noticed. A conversation had been had. Kwame had said he was fine.

What finally brought him to seek help was not a single event but a particular evening when he stood in the restaurant's walk-in refrigerator for eleven minutes because it was the only enclosed space where he could not hear the street. He had recognised, in that moment, that something had to change. He arrived at the intake appointment hoping, above everything, to feel less like a stranger inside his own life — and most afraid that the clinician would confirm what he already suspected: that the person he had been before that night was simply gone.
